notes.meaning: God calls Jerusalem to wake up from her sadness and put on royal, festive clothes. Her time of punishment and weakness has ended, and God offers her His own strength. Wicked invaders who worship false idols will never again enter to ruin and defile the holy city.

differ.view: Some hold that the promise that the unclean will never enter the city will only be literally fulfilled in the future during Christ's earthly kingdom or in the new Jerusalem, while others see it as a picture of the spiritual purity of the church.

notes.meaning: God tells captive Jerusalem to brush off the dirt of mourning and rise to her feet. Instead of sitting on the ground like a helpless slave, she is invited to sit on an honorable seat like a queen. Her days in heavy prisoner chains are over, and she is called to live in freedom.

The Lord reminds His people that they were handed over to foreign rulers without any money being paid for them. Because Babylon paid nothing to buy them, God owes the captors nothing and will redeem them without paying a ransom. This points to the free gift of salvation in Christ, which costs us nothing because Jesus paid for it with His own blood.

Long ago, Israel went down to Egypt merely as temporary guests during a famine, yet the rulers there cruelly enslaved them. Later, the Assyrians also attacked and crushed the people without any fair reason. God delivered them from both of those mighty empires in the past, showing He can easily rescue them from Babylon now.

God looks at His people suffering in exile and asks what reason He has to stay back any longer. The foreign rulers boast over the captives and cause them to cry out in deep pain. Worst of all, the enemies mock and insult God's name all day, falsely claiming He is too weak to save His followers.

Because His holy name was mocked, the Lord promises that His people will come to know who He truly is through personal experience. When the day of rescue arrives, they will know without doubt that God keeps every promise He makes. When He speaks deliverance, He is personally present to carry it out.

A runner hurries over the hilltops carrying the best news possible to a ruined city. The messenger announces peace, rescue, and the glorious truth that Zion's God reigns as King over all things. The New Testament applies this happy picture to ministers who share the good news of salvation through Jesus Christ.

Sentinels standing on the city walls call out with loud cheers and sing together for pure joy. They see clearly with their own eyes that the Lord is returning home to dwell in Zion. The promises that were once seen only from far away are now happening right in front of them.

differ.view: Some understand seeing eye to eye in the common everyday sense of watchmen being in perfect agreement, while others read the original words as meaning they visibly see the Lord face to face at close range.

notes.meaning: Even the broken stone heaps and ruins of Jerusalem are called to join in the joyful song. The Lord has brought true comfort to His hurting people by rescuing them and buying them back from slavery. When God heals what is broken, the result is full and shared thanksgiving.

The Lord rolls up His sleeve like a mighty warrior stepping onto the battlefield to defend His people. His holy power is displayed openly before every nation on earth. People in the most distant corners of the world will witness the rescue that only God can bring.

God commands the exiles to pack up and leave Babylon without keeping any of its dirty idols or corrupt customs. The priests and Levites who carry the sacred temple items back home must be especially careful to keep their lives clean and pure before the Lord. This reminds believers today to turn away from sinful habits and live holy lives.

The people will not have to rush away in terrified panic like their ancestors did when fleeing Egypt. They will march in peaceful confidence because the Lord goes out ahead to lead them along the right road. The God of Israel also guards their back, protecting them from behind so no enemy can harm them.

God points everyone to His Servant, Jesus the Messiah, promising that His great mission will succeed. Even though terrible pain comes first, God will raise Him up and grant Him the highest place of honor in heaven. His wise obedience leads directly through the cross to His resurrection and eternal reign.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that the Servant in this passage originally represented the whole nation of Israel during exile, or a specific ancient prophet like Jeremiah, rather than an individual future Messiah.

notes.meaning: Crowds were stunned and horrified when they saw how dreadfully the Servant was abused and beaten. His face and body were bruised and cut so badly that He barely looked like a human being anymore. This accurately foretells the brutal beatings, mocking, and crown of thorns Jesus endured before His death.

Just as crowds were once shocked by His pain, many nations will now be cleansed by His priestly work. Powerful kings will fall completely silent in awe when they see His rising glory. They will finally understand God's wonderful plan of salvation, which no human teacher had ever explained to them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern translators render the Hebrew word for sprinkle as startle or cause to leap, meaning the Servant will make whole nations jump in breathless astonishment at His sudden greatness.
